utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is July -- Tuesday, July 6, and I welcome the representatives of the OTP, Mr. Seselj, and everyone helping us. Today's hearing will be devoted to a videolink with a witness, a witness who is in Belgrade, and we'll look into this later on. But before this, I have an urgent problem to solve. Could we please move into closed session, Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're now in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we are currently in open session. Can you give me your first name, last name, and date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Nenad Jovic. I was born on the 2nd of October, 1957, in Radalj, near Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current occupation or do you not have a job at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now my request for an invalid's pension is being processed, so I'm unemployed at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you have the solemn declaration in your hands, I shall ask you to read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Should I stand up?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you can, you may stand up. Otherwise, you may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir, you may sit down. Sir, I shall explain to you how this hearing will unfold. The hearing will last two days. The Judges, whom you can see on the screen, will put questions to you. We have planned an hour and a half questions, i.e., 30 minutes per Judge. Once this is finished, the Prosecutor will put questions to you, and the Prosecutor will have one hour and a half. Mr. Seselj will also have one hour and a half to put questions to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first question now, and it's a very straightforward one: Sir, we have realised, on looking at the entire case file we have, that you have made several statements as of 2003 onwards. After that, you were interviewed on several occasions by the OTP; until 2007, approximately. And then all of a sudden, in 2007 you held press conferences before the Serb media in which you indicated that you were a Defence witness for Mr. Seselj. You also drafted a statement for the benefit of Mr. Seselj's Defence on the 29th of January, 2007. Could you explain to us what has happened? How is it that we have the feeling that you were initially a Prosecution witness, and from 2007 onwards you became a Defence witness? What has happened in the meantime? Can you shed some light on this for us, please?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I can explain this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't hear the witness now at all. The official did something for me here, and now I can't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall check this. Just wait a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain this. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a moment, please. We need to check that Mr. Seselj's microphone is working properly. You may begin your explanation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The problem is that I can't hear the witness. Now the volume has been put up by the usher, and it's so loud that it's intolerable. That's not the problem. The problem is that I can't hear the witness. I heard him a minute ago, when the headphones were connected to a different source.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please begin your explanation, and we'll see whether Mr. Seselj can hear you or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll answer the question. I can explain why there was this change with respect to the statements.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear him now. Apparently, there was something that was preventing me from hearing him. Did the witness actually say something? He said something very briefly. Could the witness say something now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could he say anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please say something so that we can check whether Mr. Seselj can hear you or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear him now. I was listening to him from the outset by plugging this into a different source, but a minute ago I couldn't hear the witness at all. I heard everyone, apart from the witness, and now I can hear the witness again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's working now. Witness, please tell us again why you switched from being a Prosecution witness to a Defence witness. What happened, actually?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, please be patient so that I can explain this to you in detail. I want to testify truthfully, and I wouldn't want any lies to become public -- to be disseminated amongst the public. I didn't intend to become a Prosecution witness. I was interviewed in a very inappropriate way by investigators, and for 14 hours, in fact. There were threats. I was blackmailed. My family was threatened too. I was threatened with prison. I was offered money. I was offered the possibility of staying in a hotel in Holland if I would learn by heart a statement that had already been drafted against Seselj. I was offered six months in a hotel in Holland. I was to learn a statement that had been written by heart. I said I would spend time with beautiful girls, and an associate, Predrag, said, You can avail yourself of their services at the expense of the Tribunal. And then I was told I would be taken to the Tribunal and that I could observe the proceedings through the glass, I could observe the witnesses against Seselj, so that I could get over my nervousness, so that I could face him, because he's a PhD -- he has a PhD, and, well, this was to overcome my nervousness. I was also offered the possibility of going to a third country. I was offered a lot of money. And, finally, Rita told me, Well, think about your children a little bit, and I was quite revolted by this, so I couldn't sleep. I went -- I was afraid that something would happen to my children. I had many problems with him: I threw papers down in front of her. She returned them to me, I returned them to her. Finally, I said, Madam, I'm a free man. I can leave the premises. She said, Go ahead, sir, but as soon as you go through the gate, I'll call your Ministry of the Interior and ask them to arrest you at the gate. You will then be detained in the Central Prison, and you will wait for me to come to interview you there. And we have premises where a spotlight will be directed at you. I wasn't afraid of that, I wasn't afraid of that, because I knew no one could do that to me. And, finally, I got up. I wanted to leave. She said, You'll go with me tomorrow, go back. You'll go to The Hague. You'll sing the song you have to sing there. You'll see. I was to sign what she told me. I had to sign what she told me so that I wouldn't be brought to The Hague, so that I wouldn't be accused of not respecting the Court. She threatened to bring an indictment against me. I'm not a very educated man. I can't know whether she's in a position to bring an indictment against me. Similarly, I didn't know whether she could issue a wanted request for me; that I'm not guilty, that I'm not under investigation. I worked in Montenegro. She issued a wanted notice against me. I returned home, and then I was told -- I spoke to Rita. I issued a wanted notice, but it was a mild one. I would have been happy to be arrested in Montenegro, in the Montenegro MUP. 60 per cent of the staff are Albanians. I'd have been beaten up there. While The Hague Tribunal was looking for me, the Albanians would arrest me. I'm not financially well off. I couldn't sue Ms. Rita, but that should be done. She has violated the regulations of the Tribunal. I'm sure she's violated the Rules of International Law as well. And that's why I'm saying that I never said that I would testify in this manner, but she insisted I had to sign everything that she presented me with because I was forced. I was told I would be arrested, I would be taken to The Hague by plane. I was afraid. There was blackmailing. There were threats that were made. Five or six meetings where she acted aggressively against me. I'd like to confront her, to see her face to face, to see whether this is, in fact, the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have noted everything you have said. Someone else will look into this matter. However, Witness, on the 21st of September, 2007 -- the 1st of October, 2007, you met members of the OTP. You then signed a statement. At that time, you told them that you had met members of the Serbian Radical Party, that you had met Mr. Seselj's associates. You give their names; Pop-Lazic, Radeta, Krasic. You said that they had taken down your statement. You also mentioned Janko Lakic, and you also stated that the people who had interviewed you wanted you to discredit the investigators of the OTP. Paragraph 18 of your statement is where this can be found. On reading this, one has the feeling that at that time you are saying that you gave your statement to Mr. Seselj's investigators, actually, because you were under pressure. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: There's quite a lot I'd like to say about that. I am glad that you've asked me this question. There's something I have to explain, too, with regard to that statement. I socialised with Janko Lakic from Mali Zvornik. Because of some kind of trade in nails, I owed him some money, 3.000 convertible marks. Someone came to confiscate my house, to throw me out, me and my family from my house. He said he would send someone to kill me in my house with a baseball bat or by beating me up, and he said that my wife and children would be thrown out of the house. He mentioned some names, but I wouldn't want to mention these names because people are perhaps not aware of this. Perhaps they were just trying to frighten me. I went to plead with him, ask him not to do this, to leave me alone because I had two children, I can't live in the street, I didn't have money for a flat or to survive. I have an example. With regard to Stevan Tadic, he took part of his bar and certain auxiliary buildings, and he bribed a witness to do this. I was also afraid that he would seize my house in this manner. So when I went to see him, he said, I'll forgive you for everything, but you have to be with me against the Radical Party. You have to write down what I tell you to write down. I didn't think this would ever happen, but I did what I did, and now we see that this has caused significant problems. I wrote a letter to Vojislav Seselj, the letter that he dictated to me. I did what he asked me to do. Then he mentioned this programme on B-92 Radio, and I said that I wouldn't participate in this programme. I then had a second statement that was drafted for Seselj's Defence team. Believe me, when children are at stake, you don't choose the means you have recourse to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the commercial dispute in which you were involved with Mr. Lakic, where you were threatened, as you said, Mr. Lakic wanted you to testify for Mr. Seselj or against Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Against Mr. Seselj, against Mr. Seselj, and I had to accept this for the sake of my children and my family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why was Mr. Lakic at loggerheads with Mr. Seselj; on what grounds?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know why. He also gave a statement for Seselj's Defence team. Later, there was some local problems between him and some local people up there. He wrote some sort of letters for the party. He complained -- he made complaints, and finally he decided to directly attack the Serbian Radical Party and Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of this is extremely complex. Someone will have to look into this from beginning to end and in detail. Witness, this will be one of my last questions before my colleagues put questions to you on the merits of this case. According to the documents I have, in December 2007 an article was published in "Pravda" about the fact that you did not wish to lie or say anything against Seselj, that you wanted to tell the truth. And at that time, Mr. Vucic, who was one of Mr. Seselj's associates at the time, purportedly said that you were a Defence witness. Mr. Vucic then said that he had heard this because Mrs. Natasa Kandic had purportedly told this to the press, to television. Do you remember anything about this? And if you do, can you tell us anything about it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that. I can explain this to the extent of my knowledge. It's not just rumour; it's what I know. On the 29th of November, there was a programme on the Fox Channel in Belgrade. It was called "Tell the People." Aleksandar Vucic participated in it, and the director of humanitarian law, Natasa Kandic. Natasa Kandic mentioned my name in the course of the programme. She said, You'll see what Nenad Jovic will tell you when he appears there. I'm not going to pose any questions. I'll just comment on this. If Natasa Kandic is an employee of The Hague Tribunal, she also has to be convicted for violating the Tribunal. If not, she has to give -- be given a double sentence, 14 years. I'm not going to look for her and try to prove that I'm not a criminal, but I will sue her and justice will have to be done. But let's go back to Vucic. I had contact with the Serbian Radical Party by phone. Some woman answered. I was looking for some lawyer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Sir, you are now addressing a key question, and I would like you to reflect on this before you answer. When you contacted the Serbian Radical Party, were you the person who called them up or did they call you up?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I, Nenad Jovic, phoned the Serbian Radical Party. I asked for assistance. If it had to do with the testimony of some other party, I wouldn't have contacted the Radical Party. I would have phoned the party that was involved in the proceedings. I'm not a member, with all due respect, Seselj and the other members of the party, I'm not a member of the Radical Party. I'm a member of the Movement for -- Bogoljub Karadzic's movement, the Movement for Unified Serbia. I don't know, we have the name somewhere. It's no longer in existence anymore because he was expelled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. My last question, sir: You're telling us today, under oath, that you gave statements to the Prosecutor because the Prosecution pressured you, and after that, you then contacted Mr. Seselj's Defence to tell them that you were available to testify?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have I summed up your position?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. Can you tell us today, under oath, that you gave statements to the OTP because you were being pressured by the OTP? After that, you contacted Mr. Seselj's Defence in order to testify on his behalf? Does the situation look like this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: That's how things are, but the statements didn't follow on each other that closely. It's not as if I gave the Prosecution a statement on one day and on the next day a statement for the Defence. I thought about the matter. I thought about my honour, my reputation. And if one's life is at stake, well, then so be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of your own volition, did you not at some point contact the OTP? Witness, I don't wish to trick you into anything, but according to a document I have, on the 17th of June, 2003, you, yourself, contacted the OTP in Belgrade. You, yourself, endeavoured to do this. This is the subject of a statement written by an OTP investigator. What do you have to say to that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That was Ms. Rita's interpretation too. I was called to go to the Street of Jevrema Grujica. I was called at home, and I went there. I then lost the information. On the second occasion, I asked the official to write down the request so that I had a justification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, it's an either/or situation. Either you are telling us the truth or it is the OTP investigator who is making a false statement, because the OTP investigator states as follows in his statement. Let me read it out: "On the 17th of June, 2003, the witness voluntarily contacted the OTP and let us know that they should consider him as a potential witness." The OTP is telling us, therefore, that it is you who contacted them, and not the other way 'round, as you have just told us. What do you have to say to this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: All I can say is that against the OTP -- well, I'm not against the Tribunal or the OTP. I'm impartial. I'm a witness for the truth, but I'm against the Prosecutors who meddled in that former Yugoslavia of ours, and the whole Hague Tribunal and those Prosecutors over there. The truth is what I'm telling you. I was brought an invitation, without a signature, requesting me to attend an interview in such and such a place at such and such a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're saying, and you're under oath, that you did not contact the OTP, you did not approach them. It is the OTP which sent you an invitation. What you are saying goes against the statement of 7/4/2010 which I have in my blue file. So I can show it to Mr. Marcussen in this blue file. So you say that you were served an invitation. Now, later on, did you ever call the OTP on the phone, the Belgrade Field Office, to tell them what was happening?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand those last two words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. Did you ever, yourself, call the OTP by phone to say this is happening? Did you ever do this? Did you ever call the OTP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not. I didn't know the telephone number. I was given the address, telling me where to come. And just like any other honest citizen, I abide by the rule of law and the Constitution of the state and the Tribunal, and I responded to the call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document which Mr. Marcussen knows well, on page 7, paragraph (r), it says the following: "On November 30th, 2007, the witness," i.e., you, "contacted staff at the Sarajevo Field Office," because you heard that your name had been mentioned on a television programme relating to Mr. Seselj's trial. This is what is written in the statement made by the OTP. Now, on November 30th, 2007, did you ever call the OTP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: But there was a mistake there. You said "in Sarajevo." At least that's what I heard. That was what was interpreted, that on the 30th I was in Sarajevo because of some reporting or calling up of the Tribunal, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document I have, the OTP had your cellphone number. And as of December 7, 2007, you cut off your mobile phone, and they were unable to contact you after that. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I remember that. The 7th of December; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was after the 29th of November, when Natasa Kandic disclosed to me -- or mentioned my name in the programme Fox -- or the programme called "Tell the People" on television. Now, after they told me to bring in my passport for a visa, I was never told, Listen here, you're going to be a witness. I was told that the trial would never come about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me finish this off. Of course, I could ask you questions for hours on end, but let me put to you one last question. It seems that in November 2007, you were approached by a person called Novak Savic, and this Novak Savic would be -- was probably a member of Mr. Seselj's Defence team, and he told you that you should go to Dubai, where the son of the fugitive Karadzic was residing. The son's name is Luka. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Novak Savic did his best -- since Novak Savic and I are good friends, he did his best to find me a job, because I was left jobless, and no money, either, and I can only be grateful to him and to apologise that his name isn't mentioned in that context in the statement. It was a question of interpreters. Interpreters or translators very often get things wrong. "Chetnik," well, "Chetnik," you can say Chetnik is my son, who is 11 years old, because Chetniks, they should be Serbs. Well, people talking about that should be impartial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, you're saying that Mr. Savic offered you a job. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was looking for a job. I had no money. I was working in Belgrade with some thieves who never paid me. They didn't pay me for six months. So I said, Find me a job, please, because he was a friend of mine, you see. Novak Savic is a friend of mine. He moves around a lot, so I asked him to see what he could do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is Mr. Savic a member of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: What is he? Is he a member of the Serbian Radical Party; is that what you asked me?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's my question.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I think he is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me now give the floor to my fellow Judges, because time is running. I'm sure my fellow Judges will have questions on the merits of the case. Judge Harhoff will start.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, I'm going to put some questions to you in relation to the statements that you have offered to the Prosecution, simply for the purpose of trying to find out what happened at the time in the former Yugoslavia. You have explained to the Prosecution that you volunteered as a member of first the Chetnik Movement and subsequently to the Serbian Radical Party, and that the result of this was that you were suggested as a volunteer to take part in the armed conflict in order to support the interests of the Serbian nation, and eventually you were sent off to the front-line at several locations. My first question to you, Mr. Jovic, is whether you were offered any military training, including the use of weapons and military tactics, while you were preparing for being dispatched to the front-line. Can you explain to us the background of your training?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Before I give you an answer, I have to say, with all due respect, that you made a mistake. You read something out that might have been written erroneously. I wasn't chosen or forced or elected, just pulled out to go to the front. I was a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement when the war broke out in the Republic of Croatia. I went there of my own free will because I have uncles there and relatives there. I don't want to state their names, to avoid making problems for them. But, anyway, I went of my own free will. And before I left, we did not have any training. We did not have any training, but we had to bring in our military booklet, saying that we had done our military service. And in that booklet, as a regular thing, you would see whether somebody was ill, suffered from something, had served the army, and so on. And then there would be an interview. We would talk to someone from the Crisis Staff to see what our mental state was and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. And how long a time was it since you had completed your military service?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I started my military service in 1976 and completed it in 1978. So in calender terms, it spanned three years, although the national service was 15 months, but I went in November and completed it in February 1978.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. But since the time you completed your military service and until 1991, there would have passed a substantial number of years, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, once you learn to swim, you never forget that, and it's the same thing. If you undergo 15 months of training and carry a rifle, then you would be able to do it again. I would be able to carry the same rifle I did in 1976. You can't be that forgetful and forget something that is the most important thing in your life, which is the defence of your homeland.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Well enough. Mr. Jovic, you then explained to the Prosecution that after your first deployment to the front-line, you decided, and I think it was in August 1991, that you no longer wanted to serve as a member of the SRS volunteer unit. Can you explain to us why you decided to leave?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't decide to leave the unit I was in, if it is the unit in the village of Tenja, where we were in 1991, if that's what you mean. My wife, she is deceased, but she called me to say that our child was ill. I had a daughter. She was, I think, four or five years old at the time. And I asked my commander, the commander of the Territorial Defence, to give me permission to leave the war zone to visit my child. I was given permission. I went home. However, it turned out that my wife was just very afraid for me and for my life and just wanted me home, and used that as a pretext. She was afraid for my life. And so I returned two or three days later. I don't remember exactly. I went back to the village of Tenja, but I didn't find my unit there anymore. I had to report to the defence commander, Jovo Rebraca, to say that I was back, and he told me, Your unit has been relocated for strategic reasons and moved to another place. Do you wish to stay here or do you want to follow your unit and go where they are? Now, I thought it was dangerous for me to pass through this war area, and I had got to know the locals well, so I said that I would prefer to stay on, and they took me on. So at my own responsibility, without reporting to anybody, I remained in the village of Tenja, and I don't know where the others were and where they went to. I no longer met them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did Mr. Rebraca tell you why the SRS unit had left Tenja?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He said that it was for strategic reasons that they were being redeployed, moved to another area. For strategic reasons, he said, and he was the commander. So I didn't have an insight into the situation on the ground. He told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You then went on to explain that at a later point in time, you were dispatched to somewhere in Bosnia. And you also told us or told the Prosecution that the transportation was arranged through the hydroelectric plants in the area, which provided drivers and some vehicles. Can you clarify the details of the transportation to this new place?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I remember it well. If it was anything false -- well, actually, you didn't ask the full question. It was a transport of volunteers to the village of Darda. Now, since that's the truth, then I can tell you about it. If it wasn't the truth, I wouldn't be telling you about it. So we have the village of Darda. Well, when I was in Tenja and came back home from Tenja, Janko Lakic came to see me and asked me whether I would like to go to the village of Darda, in Baranja, because I was a tried-and-tested fighter already, and to take a group with me, a group of volunteers; to test their metel, young guys, they like to do that. And I said I did want to go, but I didn't want to be the command or responsible for anybody's life. And he said the unit belonging to the MUP of Republika Srpska -- no, not Republika Srpska, the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. It's Republika Srpska now. Anyway, that we should go through them. I didn't mind who I went through. I was used to war, so I could go. I would have to mention a name here. Should we go into private session or should I keep quiet?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. Harhoff. You said "to Bosnia." This was Baranja. Baranja is in the Republika Srpska Krajina, and we're dealing with 1991 there, whereas Bosnia, the war was from April 1992, in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you for pointing this out. Indeed, I was mistaken. Baranja is in Croatia. I'm aware of that. But my question was really a different one, and this is why I don't think it's necessary to go into private session, Mr. Jovic. My question was: Who organised the transportation? Was that the hydroelectric plant that you mentioned to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No. The transportation was organised and probably paid for by the MUP or the junior commander, the then MUP commander in Zvornik, so across in Bosnia. They just used their buses. They were minibuses; not many people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But how come that the MUP would dispose over the buses belonging to a private company?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they would rent them out. If I'm a private person, I can rent out 10 buses if I have somebody to drive, and an institution like the MUP and the MUP commander could do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Okay. So I understand that the transportation was provided for by the MUP and that the MUP had rented buses from the hydroelectric plant. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's it, precisely, and the unit belonged to the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You then go on to mention an episode in November, at the end of November 1991, a week before you left Baranja. And you mention an episode in which Rade Kostic approached you and asked you to become a member of the police in Darda. And from what I understood from your statements, you seem to indicate that Mr. Kostic was asking the group that you were with if they wanted to give up their Chetnik appearance and become members of the police, or whether they wanted to stay as Chetniks. And I was left with the impression that somehow Mr. Kostic was not very pleased with the volunteers and so would not be willing to admit anyone who insisted on appearing as a Chetnik into the police force. Can you clarify these events? In other words, is it correct --

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I can clarify that. Mr. Kostic said that anybody who wanted to remain in the police force, because we were already in police uniform and we acted as policemen, we were working as policeman. And what you said about giving up the Chetnik appearance, we were all policemen in the first place. We were neat, clean-shaven, our hair was cut properly, because we belonged to the MUP. So there was no other appearance, no other markings or personal traits. We looked like the MUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But why then would Mr. Kostic ask you to take off Chetnik symbols and insignia from the uniforms, and why would he insist that only those who were willing to give up these appearances could stay in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was the interpretation of the person that wrote that down. On oath, I claim that we did not have any appearance of that kind. I am proud of having the Chetnik symbols and insignia, but at the time we were without that. We were clean-shaven, our hair was neatly cut, we wore MUP uniforms, and the whole village of Darda can testify to that. They're all over Serbia now. You can find them in all the villages. But, anyway, they would be happy to testify to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, Mr. Kostic would not have made any special reference to his unwillingness to include Chetniks into the police force; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you see Chetniks? I do apologise for having to ask you that, but where do you see Chetniks? We didn't come as Chetniks, we didn't look like Chetniks. They dressed us in police uniforms, with police insignia. We belonged to the MUP of Krajina; not the MUP of Serbia, but the MUP of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I understand. While you were in Darda, and while you were serving there as a police -- as a member of the MUP, who paid you for your services?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: We were volunteers. Nobody paid us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I suppose you would have to live on something. Didn't you receive any payment from either the party or the MUP or the TO or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. As volunteers, we were given accommodation and food, and nothing more than that. And the party -- well, let me mention that we had nothing to do with the Radical Party, or the Democratic Party, or any other party, for that matter, in Serbia while we were over there. So I state with full responsibility that that was how it was. I know what happened, I know what the truth was, and I am a witness here to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And later on, did you receive any payment from the SDS Party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I, personally, later on did, but -- well, only I, personally, I, Nenad Jovic, personally, went with the commander -- with the police commander. Well, I was there all the time. I was in the security detail. And from the SDS, I received remuneration in the form of assistance, because I wasn't employed anywhere and I had to be present over there for a time. Perhaps for two months, not even two months; less. But as a policeman, as a reservist, police reservist. That was on the ready there. Because the MUP was divided, the chief was a Muslim, the commander was a Serb, and you couldn't receive a salary from them directly. You couldn't tell a Muslim, Now you have to pay this man for helping us out. It went through the party, so that I had some financial assistance, and so that I can have it certified and talk about it. Maybe I shouldn't, but that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Were the police reservists not paid by the MUP while they were on service -- while they were in service, when they were called up from the reserve ranks?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: The reservists were, but I was not listed as -- well, the chief was a Muslim, as I said, so to bring me in the reserve police force, it was very difficult and not an opportune thing to do, because I was from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But you told us just a minute ago that you were a police reservist, so why wouldn't you be paid, as anybody else, by the MUP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I said a police reservist so that you should not think that I was an active-duty policeman working in Zvornik. By agreement with the chief of the police station, I was his personal security detail. I drove him around. If necessary, I worked in civilian clothes, checking around town, who was purchasing weapons, selling weapons. I would collect information and went to the Serb Command, because there was a lot of weapons trafficking, the Muslims -- weapons. Well, so did the Serbs, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you have told us that you were a police reservist. You have also confirmed that police reservists were paid by the MUP for the time they were in active service. Yet you also explain to us that you received payment from the SDS Party. So I'm left with an impression that there was a confusion of the authority vested in the MUP and the authority vested in the political party. Or did you serve two masters, simply?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're right. But you're not right when you say that I said that I, as a reservist, received a salary. I didn't receive such a salary from the MUP. I was with the commander. I acted as his escort. I have already explained that. If you like, I'll repeat it. It's not difficult for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You do not need to repeat, and I did understand that you were not paid by the MUP, but you were occasionally paid by the SDS while you were serving as a police reservist, and this is what confuses me. And my conclusion is that you probably were serving two masters, and this is what I would like you to comment on.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand how I was serving two masters. If I've understood you correctly, you said that I was serving two masters; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That was my question. And if I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which two masters --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Hold on. Let me finish my question with the witness and then you can intervene. You were working or functioning as a police reservist, and yet you were paid by the SDS. How does this fit together?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I comment on the interpretation, Mr. Harhoff? The interpretation is not correct. You said, according to the transcript in English, "serving two masters." This can be interpreted into the Serbian language as "you were serving two owners or employers." An employer is one thing, and a master is something else. But the interpreter doesn't know the Serbian language, and that is why we have a problem. If you had told the witness "two proprietors" or "two employers," then he would have known what you meant. When you said "two masters," well, that confuses the witness. So the interpreter can laugh as much as she likes, but she doesn't know the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I am not a Serbian native speaker, so I have no idea about the correct translation or interpretation of what I told you. But with Mr. Seselj's comments, Mr. Jovic, are you able to answer my question? My question relates to the fact that you were working as a police reservist and yet paid by someone else than the MUP.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but at the time I wasn't mobilised as a reserve policeman. I was working by escorting or, rather, providing security to the commander, at his personal request. I wasn't asked to come and work as a reserve policeman. It was a personal request. You understand there was a private agreement, Will you come, work with me. I had one boss, so that's what confused me. That's why I was unable to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Now I am even more confused, because now you tell us that you weren't really a police reservist, although you were wearing a police uniform, but you were working more or less on a private basis as a bodyguard, I understand, and yet still paid by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: We don't understand each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Probably not. I am asking you to explain to us how it came that you were wearing a police uniform, but you were not actually working as a police reservist, but as a bodyguard to a police chief, and you were paid by the SDS. How do these three functions fit together?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's very easy to explain this. I worked in the civilian sector --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, can I interrupt you, because I want to make sure that you do not understand my questions as in any way trying to lead you into a trap or something. That is certainly not my intention. The only information that I'm looking for is what the relations were between the MUP and the political parties, and the authority that apparently a police commander would have to employ someone more or less on a private basis to protect him.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, naturally, war was imminent. The man didn't feel safe. I'd spent a lengthy period of time at the front, and he wanted to have someone by his side who would be able to protect him if there was an attack, because fire would be opened in villages, there would be bursts of fires at night, and so on and so forth. So this was probably the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to have a break now, and we shall resume later on. The Registrar has turned around several times and looked at me to indicate this to me. We are going to have a 20-minute break. Please have a good rest, and we shall meet against in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The court is back in session. I would like to state for the record that the first few minutes of today's hearing were in open session and not in closed session. Judge Harhoff will continue putting his questions now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As the Registrar has asked me to do, after these two minutes that were in open session, we then moved into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to make a brief comment again, Mr. President. Before the end of the first session, you said that the Registrar was telling you that the time was up and that we had to have a break, and the interpreter said the witness gave you a sign indicating that it was time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having specified this. I did not understand that the witness told us that it was time to have a break. Thank you. Anyway, Witness, we shall continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. I think we, in the interests of time, should move on to something else. You mentioned to the Prosecution that during the attack on Zvornik, there were some 40 men participating under the command of Arkan, and you also said that there were some 30 to 40 men under the command of a gentleman called Zuco. Do you recall this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I'm certain I didn't say that about Zuco, because I heard about Zuco for the first time after the liberation of the town of Kula, and that was 14 or 15 days later. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Right. Do you know if any of these 30 to 40 Chetniks, who you said took part in the attack on Zvornik, were SRS volunteers, and was Zuco a member of the SRS?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say they were Chetniks. And, secondly, I've already said that Zuco is someone I didn't even know at the time. I hadn't heard of him, not until the liberation of the town of Kula, which is part of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: To be more direct, then, Mr. Jovic, let me ask you directly. Did any of the SRS volunteers, or Seselj's men, as they came to be known, take part in the attack on Zvornik? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether they participated. But in the attack, there were people wearing cockade hats. There were some people from Zvornik who'd been driven out over the barricades, and some people from Karakaj, near Zvornik. I knew some of them personally. They were just across the Drina River. I know half of Zvornik even now. There was no one from outside, apart from Arkan's unit and myself, who turned up then. Then there was the Serbian police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, we have that in your statement. But just to conclude what you just said on the Chetniks in the attack, or the persons wearing cockades in the attack on Zvornik, you don't know if any of these were members of the SRS and you don't know whether they were under the command of Mr. Zuco; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. And I know for sure that I didn't see Zuco or hear about him until the operation to liberate Kula, which is part of the town of Zvornik. When Zvornik was liberated, well, that didn't mean that the entire area was liberated. Kula is adjacent to Zvornik, and that's where that place was under threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Let's just for a second have a look at the liberation of Kula. Did you then learn or did you receive any information of whether Mr. Zuco had any relationship with the SRS?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: What I heard of Zuco -- about Zuco after the liberation of the town of Kula, I knew that they belonged to some independent unit. I didn't see such volunteers, though, but perhaps they were in a different position on the other side, somewhere else. But they weren't in the town. I never heard that Zuco was a member of the SRS. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but I never heard about that, because I didn't even know Zuco at the time. If he were a close friend of mine, I would know. I would say, yes, he was, or, no, he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. So can we conclude that in your testimony, you did not know whether Zuco or any of his men had anything to do with the SRS or with Seselj? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: The only conclusion I can draw is that Zuco wasn't a member of the Serbian Radical Party, because there were colleagues who worked at the bridge, and I heard from them that after the fall of Kula, the SRS volunteers all withdrew. But Zuco remained, and I know him from that time. If he had been a volunteer of the SRS, he would have had to leave with his men, and some of his individual combatants would certainly have been punished. We were controlled. Zoran Rankic came to see us to see what discipline was like, to see whether we obeyed orders, to ensure that we weren't causing the local inhabitants any problems. You probably know what happened with Zuco later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We do. Thank you very much. Let's move forward to your reference to the Chetniks protecting some of the bridges in Zvornik. And I think you explained to the Prosecution that the Chetniks who were manning the posts at the bridges were searching people, not only Muslims, but also Serbs, and that they were stealing, and for that reason they were expelled shortly after or removed from those check-points. Can you clarify why the Chetniks who were securing the bridges were removed from that duty?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Those people weren't Chetniks, sir. There were two groups of men. There was one group that was securing the bridges. They were flexible with regard to the citizens, at least in that town, because we were there, the police were there with them. And later there was some sort of unofficial group. They had come there of their own accord. They were there for a certain number of days, and they were driven away by Commander Panic. Rumours were that they would strip women, but this group was formed of vagrants from various villages. It wasn't Zvornik or other group. One -- some was from Zvornik, another from Krupa, they were perhaps from various places. I didn't see them and I can't say anything about them. I wasn't involved in the attack on Kula. I was involved in the attack -- or, rather, I was on leave. I went to Novi Sad and stayed there with my relative. I was there for a week so I can't really say. I'm not in a position to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: We'll get to Kula in just a second. Can I just conclude the question that I have on Zvornik by asking you: Who, to your knowledge, was leading the attack on Zvornik; do you know?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff from Zvornik led the attack on Zvornik. At the time, the Republika Srpska wasn't in existence, but the Crisis Staff of Serbs from Zvornik was involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: And who was the operational commander?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know who the operational commander was. There was the Crisis Staff commander. Who else would there have been?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: You seem to have indicated in your statements to the Prosecution that the attack was led by Arkan, as the commander, and this was just a question to confirm whether you stood by this. Let's move, then, to Kula, and that will be my final questions, because you said that when finally the attack on Kula was about to begin, you had noticed that the way in which the attack was organised was such that literally all or at least most of the Muslim inhabitants in Kula would be killed, or the non-Serb -- sorry, the non-Serb inhabitants in Kula would be killed, and for that reason, you refused to take part. Can you explain the events surrounding the attack on Kula?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can explain the events, although I didn't participate in the operation to liberate the town. I call this an operation to liberate part of Zvornik because the Muslims, prior to the war, used the media, the newspapers, the television, to boast that they had Stigler [phoen] missiles, they were armed, that they had certain weapons at their disposal, so a competent team prepared to go there, naturally. But I was on leave. I couldn't go there for various reasons, because I was tired, I'd been on duty 24 hours a day in town, so I borrowed a colleague's car and went to Novi Sad to stay with my relative, my sister-in-law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So if I understand you, you did not refrain from taking part in the attack on Kula because of any concerns for the civilian population in Kula; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, an honourable combatant doesn't abuse civilians, doesn't kill civilians, but I was quite simply burnt out. I was no longer capable of participating in something like that. Because people were on duty on bridges, in streets, we worked around the clock. I said I had to leave. I said that my child was ill. I managed to get out of that situation, and I left so that I could have a rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Did you have information, actually, about the way in which the attack on Kula was organised, and did that information suggest that ultimately the non-Serb civilian population in Kula would be killed, or most of them, at least?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't have any such information because I wasn't in the Crisis Staff Command. Secondly, I didn't know how many people would be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have a follow-up question, in line with the question put by my colleague, which lies at the heart of the issue at stake here. As you know, we must try Mr. Seselj on the basis of what has happened in Zvornik. Your testimony is valuable to us, because I notice that when you gave a statement on the 18th and 19th of October, 2006, in paragraph 92 of this statement - you don't need to look at it - you explained that during the attack on Zvornik, there were 40 of Arkan's men, 15 Serbian policemen, and 50 Chetniks belonging to Seselj. You said that this group was made up of 100 to 120 people. This sentence lies heavily on the accused, because according to what you said at the time, there was something like 50 Chetniks belonging to Seselj in Zvornik. What do you have to say to this today?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: That's a matter of interpretation or of mistranslation. I said quite clearly there were about 40 of Arkan's men, about 15 or 16 -- I don't know the exact number. Fifteen or 16 policemen. Everyone else was from Zvornik and from Karakaj, a suburb of Zvornik. They had cockades on their heads. If we had unloaded a lorry of cockades, they would have disappeared in a day. And no one survived Tito's Communist regime, no one touched him, so why talk about Chetnik insignia? On the state flag used at present, we have the Nemanjic coat of arms, so it means that the president, Mr. Tadic, is a Chetnik. Does it? I don't know, we're all Chetniks now in the eyes of certain individuals. But I know that Tadic is not a Chetnik. That's quite certain. You can't judge people on the basis of the fact that they put a cockade on their heads. I didn't see any of Seselj's men. I wasn't aware of them turning up or leaving. But according to some of the statements made by Mr. Seselj here before this Tribunal, I came to understand that he had a group of his own. As to where it was active, in which territory, I don't know. Someone else must know about that, and someone else must be in a position to inform you of the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My fellow Judge, Ms. Lattanzi, has half an hour for questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I apologise, but I think we have to backtrack somehow and go back to the time when you were recruited within the Serbian Chetnik Movement in 1990. I would like to know, regarding this period of time, who exactly were the leaders of this movement.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: The leader of that movement was Janko Lakic, at a local level in the Mali Zvornik municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did he hail from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: He originated from Republika Srpska, but -- well, he lived in Serbia for 10 or 12 years. He has an apartment there by the stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you give us the year or years when he lived in Serbia? I'd like to know when he lived in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I didn't really know him before 1990, when the Serbian Chetnik Movement was -- there was this promotional ceremony in Mali Zvornik of the movement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990, he lived in Serbia, is that it, or did he live in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: In Serbia, I think. 100 per cent, I know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mrs. Lattanzi, Mali Zvornik is in Serbia, and Zvornik is in Republika Srpska, separated by the Drina River.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So he lived in Zvornik. What about Despotovic; who was it? Did he live in Mali Zvornik or did he live in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: He lived in Mali Zvornik. His wife worked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What about Despotovic, Aleksandar Despotovic? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Despotovic is -- was born in Serbia, and he lived in Serbia, and he stills lives in Serbia, just like me. I was born in Serbia and I live in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What role did he play within the Serbian Chetnik Movement in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, something like me, similar to me. I was the deputy of some president, or vice-president, or whatever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who did you obtain the certificate for recruitment within the Serbian Chetnik Movement from?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: From Janko Lakic. I received a certificate at the end of April or the beginning of May - I'm not quite sure - but on a voluntary basis, because I asked them, because those young guys were ready to fight against the five-pointed star of Milosevic and Communism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was Mr. Seselj a leader of the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj was most probably -- yes, he was the leader of the Chetnik Movement, and he held a promotional rally to promote his movement. That was held in Zvornik at the end of April or beginning of May - I'm not quite sure - in the Dom Kulture, the cultural centre building. Because I'm a local of Mali Zvornik, I could tell you the names of 300 people who attended. I wasn't able to go in myself, because there was a crowd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're talking about 1990; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, 1990, because you asked me when I became a member, and I became a member the morning after --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And after?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: The morning after the rally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What? After having heard Mr. Seselj, maybe?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't able to enter the hall because there were too many people. Lots of people were interested. So I had to stand outside, and I saw how the Muslims set up a cordon at the entrance door, waiting for the Serbs to come out. So I couldn't hear what Seselj was saying inside because there was a lot of noise when this promotional rally of the Serbian Chetnik Movement was going on. And as the people were coming out of the building, the Muslims beat them, hit them, kicked them, and the police cordon didn't do anything to stop them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Nobody told you what Mr. Seselj had said, what he talked about?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course they did. The local Muslims told me, too, who went inside to hear what he was saying; not to become a member, but they said, We want to hear everybody's platform and what they have to say, and then we can choose which party we want to belong to. I have a lot of Muslim friends in Zvornik, and I still have friends like that that come home, to my home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were the Muslims happy with Mr. Seselj's speech?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they were happy with his speech or not. A brawl broke out. Five hundred people clashed. They destroyed a bus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was there a fight? Do you know what was the reason for the fight?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Because the Muslims, three days before that, were preparing -- were collecting stones up on their balconies. Regardless of Seselj was going to say, the important thing was to hit him with stones. And a Serb told me that, well, the Muslim had cocked a pistol and wanted to shoot, and the Serbs stopped him from doing that. But the police was there in civilian clothes, and Motorolas, and they just said, Don't be afraid, this rally has been announced -- was announced in advance. And so that was it. And in the morning, I went to find Janko Lakic because I wanted to become a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement the next day, because the young guys were brave, they were courageous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But since you decided to join, you must have known that they had a platform, a programme, or did you just join because you felt sympathy towards this movement without really knowing what their platform was all about? And here I'm talking about the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Maybe the platform of the programme had been spelled out by Mr. Seselj during this rally.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear what he said at the rally, but I knew that they had the courage to sing at a rally in Belgrade, to sing songs against the five-pointed star of Communism and to shout slogans. So I liked people who had the guts to do something like that. But the police were there, and they said, We're doing our job, and they said, We're doing our job. We want to take down the five-pointed star, we want to topple the regime. We don't want to live in darkness anymore. So that was the beginning of it all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you know what was the relationship at the time between Seselj and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I knew. Well, at that time, Seselj was arrested every other day. Well, not literally every other day. I use that expression. But he would be arrested from time to time, whether in Kragujevac, or Belgrade, or wherever. So the situation was highly unfavorable, as far as Mr. Seselj was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And this relationship was always bad?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, yes. Maybe something changed when the bombings started and when a national salvation government came into power. They might have co-operated in setting up a defence, so there might have been some agreement at that level. But, otherwise, during the war from 1991 to 1995 and onwards, their relationship was extremely bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we'll now move on to the attempt in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I have a follow-up question. It's extremely important. Judge Lattanzi asked you a number of questions on this rally held in the area of Mali Zvornik, and you said that it was held in 1990. You are aware of what happened when Zvornik was attacked in 1992, so I'd like to know whether, as far as you know, Mr. Seselj had come to Zvornik or Mali Zvornik prior to the attack on Zvornik in order to make a speech, because this is what the Prosecution is stating in its indictment and in its pre-trial brief. And any Judge like me, French, Italian, or Dane, must check these allegations made by the Prosecution as well as check allegations made by the Defence, so I would like to know, as far as you know, whether a rally would have been held by Mr. Seselj just a few days before Zvornik was attacked.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I'll answer your question, but you've asked me a series of questions, in actual fact. I tend to forget, due to my illness, so I'll answer the last question and then move backwards. Now, Vojislav Seselj, in Mali Zvornik, in Serbia, in 1990, 1990, held a promotional rally of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. The Serbian Radical Party didn't exist at the time, so you can't have a witness saying that that was so. Well, you can have a witness like that, but that would be a false witness. The witness would be lying. And in SUP, the party was registered, and you can check that out. You're the Judges. You can find when the rally was registered. There was permission for the rally to be held, this promotional rally. And they provided police security, and the police did nothing. We should have beat them up, but Vojislav Seselj said, Don't touch the police, and we listened to him. Otherwise, we should have. Now, could you repeat your question? You asked me three questions, and I've answered the latter one, but could you repeat the others?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I might have been a bit lengthy, but I'd like to know the following, and it's absolutely essential. I would like to know whether Mr. Seselj held a rally in Mali Zvornik in 1992, just a few days before the attack on Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Seselj -- Vojislav Seselj held a rally -- and let me repeat again. I'm under oath here. I know the town. I was born there, I grew up there, so I know everything about the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just a minute. The Presiding Judge is asking you a question about 1992, not about 1990.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Judge, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1990, and now we're moving on to 1992. The Presiding Judge would like to know whether a rally was held in Mali Zvornik in 1992 or whether Mr. Seselj visited the area or something of the kind in the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992, even if the rally was held, I don't know whether -- I wasn't there, but you couldn't have had Muslims there. Who could have crossed the bridge in 1992 to fight in Serbia and collect up stones? There were 2.000 people there, both Serbs and Muslims. I assume that's common knowledge. It was war in 1992. And in the pre-war times, where could they go when everybody was armed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But may I be allowed to add something? We're back to the time when people were trying to get you to join the Croatian front when you were a member of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. You left by bus. There were 30 volunteers on the bus coming from Valjevo and 20 volunteers from Belgrade. Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Madame Judge, I do remember that, but you're reading something that's not true. Who could have forced me to go to the front? Only the Army of Yugoslavia, and no party. I know what military power and military command means. It's the General Staff of Yugoslavia, that's what it is. So I went to the front as a volunteer through the Radical Party because of my relatives living in what is today Croatia, so I went as a volunteer without orders from anybody. I joined up the Serbian Radical Party. Nobody forced me to join up and to sign the membership form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me say that I never mentioned any obligation that would have been imposed on you. All I said is that obviously --

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: That's the interpretation I received.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... to get you to go to the Croatian front among other volunteers. I never said that you were obliged to do this, that anyone forced you to do this. But the bus was full of volunteers, some coming from Belgrade and others, according to what you say, from Valjevo. Where is Valjevo, where is it? Is it in Serbia? Where is it located?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Madame Judge, let me just explain something to you. The interpretation I received was "how were you forced," "how did they force you," and that's why, with all due respect, I have to say, and I apologise for that, but nobody can force me to do anything, let alone some local group or board of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you that even when I look at the English transcript, it's obvious that I never talked about any obligation that you might have had. But let's put this aside and return to these volunteers, 20 hailing from Belgrade and 30 from Valjevo. Where is Valjevo?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Valjevo, in relation to Mali Zvornik, do you want me to tell you that? With respect to my place, it's 40 or 50 kilometres to the right, towards -- well, the Drina River is left, so it's the opposite side, right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Serbia?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, regarding this first attempt to get to the Croatian front: When you arrived in Belgrade, at the HQ of the Serbian Chetnik Movement, who did you find there? Were there any leaders?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were people from the Crisis Staff there, Zoran Rankic, Ljubisa Petkovic, then from time to time Dr. Vojislav Seselj would come. But I can't say that they were always there together. One would come, the other one would go. Sometimes for, say, 20 minutes, the three of them were there together, but otherwise there would be this coming and going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then there was another attempt to join the Croatian front, and if I understood things correctly, this second attempt was successful. And on that occasion, you went directly to Belgrade again, and I would like to know who was at the HQ of the Serbian Chetnik Movement.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff, the premises of the Serbian Chetnik Movement. Well, what did we come across there? We came across people working in the Crisis Staff; that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you identify these people?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... your question. I don't know. Zoran Rankic. I know that Ljubisa Petkovic was there, for instance. I can't remember whether Zoran was there. It's been a long time since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who is Golubovic, Golub, aka Golub?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Golubovic, Golub. Well, Golub is an inhabitant of Tenja. I don't know who this Golubovic is. He's a tyre repairman in the village of Tenja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You met with him directly in Tenja?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I apologise. I was a bit confused.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. Maybe I'm speaking too loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... connected to the Serbian Chetnik Movement or as of the time to the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. Maybe -- well, it's normal that they had to -- well, the Serbian Radical Party had to find a connection, somebody to take their men in there. There might have been some co-ordinator. I really don't know. All I do know is that they sent us back once --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe Jovo Rebraca would have been one of these co-ordinators, Jovo Rebraca.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Jovo Rebraca was the commander of the defence of the village of Tenja, and after the war he was mayor, the president of the municipality of Tenja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was connected to the SRS or, in general, to the Serbian Chetnik Movement?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. All I do know is that we -- when we arrived as volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party, we went to Jovo Rebraca and we were issued weapons. We didn't have any uniforms because we were poor, so no uniforms. We had some overalls and some old rifles, but just so that you could shoot once or twice and instill fear into someone. That was all they were good for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Tenja, you found Arkan's unit; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: In passing, I saw -- well, I don't know where they were stationed, but I did see them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The unit of the Serbian Chetnik -- unit of the Serbian Radical Party, you did not see that there was a co-operation with them and the operation in the field together with Arkan's unit?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Who could there have been co-operation with? Well, they were better armed, they were powerful. I apologise. It's not that I'm shouting at you. I'm speaking up so you can hear me better, and I, myself, don't hear very well. My hearing has been impaired, so it's difficult for me to control my voice. So I tend to shout a bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't worry about it. So was there any co-operation with Arkan's unit?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly not. There couldn't have been any co-operation with them because they were armed, powerful, and Arkan and Vojislav Seselj didn't see eye to eye. They were arrogant. I think they hate each other to this day. Well, the other one's dead now, but, anyway, that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why did they hate each other?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Because Seselj, Vojislav Seselj, had other views about the political life of Serbia and the war events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what was this diverging view?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they differed because the Serb Chetniks -- or, rather, the Serb Radicals were people who acted in accordance with the Geneva Conventions, for example. I never saw Arkan kill anybody, either, but these were rumours going 'round. But I didn't see anything so as to be able to testify and say they killed so many people. But there were a lot of dead bodies; that's a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you ever meet Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I just saw him when I went over there, and then never again. As a volunteer, when I went there as a volunteer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At some point, what did you talk about, if you spoke to him?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't talk to him, personally. We would sort of exchange a friendly, Good day to you, and, God be with us, and things like that, but he went about his own business and we remained there and waited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And as a group, what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat that? Could the interpreter please repeat that? As a group, well, there was some jokes. We went to the party, we were there, and we waited for contact, for transport. Rankic said that Petkovic had to find means of going there. Ljubisa Petkovic didn't want our lives to be at risk, so we had to wait for this to be secure. We weren't supposed to be angry with Ljubisa. There were people who were angry with him. They want to do beat him up. But Ljubisa was right, because we would have ended up in Borovo Naselje, perhaps, where there were only Croats, because we were going to go without weapons of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Republika Srpska was established. I wanted to know from you whether you knew anything about it. What relationship existed between the leaders of the Serbian Radical Party, and Mr. Seselj, more specifically, and the leaders of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Lattanzi, I have to intervene. Republika Srpska was established in 1992. So far, you have been discussing 1991 with the witness, just to avoid confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was at a time when the Republika Srpska was established in 1992. I need to finish in five minutes' time. This is -- you are right, I skipped over these months. I was asking the witness whether he knows anything about the relationship between Mr. Seselj and the leaders of the Republika Srpska, since you talk about it in your statements, your prior statements.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
