utterances.text: I really don't know anything about that. I'd like to know what that statement says, who interpreted that statement of mine. I'll go to Strasbourg to take legal action against the investigator. I don't know what to do with him. Certain things continue to be attributed to me as if I were an American. I can't hear anything. I don't know if you can hear me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No interpretation into the Serbian language is being received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can hear now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me repeat. This might be my mistake. Let me repeat. In one of your statements -- in two of your statements, you say that Janko Lakic, the secretary of the municipal Chetnik Movement, asked you to join a group of young men from the Republika Srpska at a time when the Republika Srpska had been established as such. Can you confirm this or not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was in 1991. That's what the story has to do with. It was in November or October 1991. What kind of Republika Srpska? War hadn't yet broken out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, the Republika Srpska had not yet been proclaimed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No. The war hadn't even broken out, Madame, in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. Therefore, there are a few problems with the statement.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I can see that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Republika Srpska existed already, may I put this question: When Janko Lakic asked you to join a group of young men, what did this have to do with? Young men from where, from what party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: They were local men from the surrounding villages. They were volunteers who, through the MUP --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mention a trip that lasted 20 days to Baranja?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but this was through the MUP. There was the command of the Serbian people who was in the Zvornik MUP in Bosnia. The chief was a Muslim; the commander was a Serb. The commander, probably in secret, organised a group to go and spend a little time at the front. We set off in police uniforms with police insignia. We were members of the police force. Everyone was cleanly shaven. We had tidy haircuts, and so on and so form. It was a police unit, the police of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. When we arrived there in Darda, we were part of that force.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To conclude, I would like to go back a little bit and discuss what you were doing in the spring of 1992. Were you in Zvornik, Mali Zvornik; yes or no? I'm talking about the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Feel free to ask me about that. My memory is defective, so I can't remember everything. Ask me whether I participated in a liberation operation or not. I'll tell you everything. I don't know what you have in mind when you ask me, What did you do? I was in Zvornik and did all sorts of things. I even had mistresses there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first of all want to know whether you were there or not, around Zvornik and Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not hear of a visit by Mr. Seselj, did you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No, no. He didn't appear there and I didn't hear of such a visit. I was present there until the beginning of the operation to liberate Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you take part in the liberation of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a while, until a man was wounded by my side. I then carried him on my back, the police of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were in the Serbian police as a volunteer?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: As a volunteer in the police force of the Serbian people of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You were a volunteer representing a particular group, a party? In other words, these volunteers had been organised by a political party or on an individual basis?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, my wife is from Bosnia, from Zvornik. I wasn't a member of any party, because the Serbian Radical Party expelled me from the party because I refused to go --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is something I know. I know you were there as a volunteer, as a private individual. Time has run out, unfortunately. I would have a lot of questions to put to you still. One last point. I would like to know why the volunteers of the Serbian Chetnik Movement were driven out of Zvornik in 1992.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't know how to answer that. The volunteers of the Serbian Chetnik Movement weren't driven out of Zvornik. That's the first thing. Zuco was driven out. I don't know in which year, but Zuco was driven out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean Zuco. He was on his own. He didn't belong to anyone. He belonged to himself. He didn't belong to the MUP. He wasn't a member of the MUP, or of the police force, or of the Radical Party. I don't know how to define him. The Yellow Wasp, that's what I could say. What that, in fact, is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, it is not true to say that they were driven out of Zvornik because they were raping women?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, raped them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't quite follow what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I didn't understand very well.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I said there are all sorts of things said in the statement, and as a result I'd convert to a different faith, but I'll do that so as not to irritate anyone once I leave these premises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is a private matter, and it's a good thing you don't do it here. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we're going to have a break now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a break, and then the Prosecutor will put his questions to you. I have a follow-up question for you. You said a while ago that you had been expelled from the Serbian Radical Party. Could you tell us why you were expelled from the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Because the rule of the Serbian Radical Party was as follows: If someone voluntarily changes his or her -- his unit, the Serbian Radical Party will no longer be responsible for him, won't have him on their list, and they can't find him then. He can be killed and they won't even know. They have to know where their men are. I remained down there without anyone being aware of the fact, so that's the only reason. I stayed on there. I was no longer one of their men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From what date onwards, exactly?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: 1991. I don't know when exactly, I really couldn't say. I'd like to answer that question, believe me, but I don't know. A certain number of days later, when I went to Rebraca, that was when, but I don't know the exact date. I'd like to answer your question, believe me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said something, despite yourself, something which is important, and you didn't notice that you were saying it. You've just said that the Serbian Radical Party wanted to know exactly where their men were located. When you said that, one has the feeling -- I might be mistaken, but one has the feeling that the Serbian Radical Party was exercising control over its members who were in different units. Is this what you have said?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I said that they would visit us to see how we were conducting ourselves, to see whether there were problems with the local inhabitants, whether we were maltreating anyone. If people drank too much, they'd take them home. Sometimes they'd bring us a pack of cigarettes. And that was it. There were no orders issued of any kind. The party can't issue such orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You anticipated my following question invariably. What I'm interested in is to know whether, from Belgrade, the Serbian Radical Party was closely controlling the activities of the members of the Serbian Radical Party or whether these units were solely placed under the control of the Territorial Defence or of the JNA. What can you say to us about this?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, when I left, the JNA had a buffer zone established there and performed UNPROFOR duties, duties similar to those that UNPROFOR had. Later on, according to what I heard, according to rumours which are true, they went to Bubanj Potok. That could be seen on the television. They would get dressed, put on uniforms, and they would be JNA members. There were no insignia of any kind, but they had JNA uniforms and everything else they needed. That was on television, and I'm familiar with that, but I wasn't present there. So, I don't know, perhaps I'm mistaken too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question -- my penultimate question: According to you, did the Serbian Radical Party know at any point in time where its volunteers were? Did they know, for instance, that X was in such and such a unit, Y in such and such another unit? Is this something -- is this something they knew permanently?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: In my opinion, they should have been aware of where their combatants were. They should have known whether the men were alive, whether someone had been arrested, whether someone had been wounded, and if so, they should be transferred to a hospital so to avoid worries of such kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question now. A while ago, my colleague mentioned the Republika Srpska to you. As far as you know, did the VRS, i.e., the Army of the Republika Srpska, commanded by General Mladic, still to be located to this day -- according to you, did the soldiers of the Republika Srpska have along side them units made up of volunteers coming from Serbia, for instance, who had remained under the control of the JNA or of the political parties in Serbia? Is that a possibility or not?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I only spent about seven months down there in Zvornik, so you could ask someone in a bar whether this was possible or not. But Ratko Mladic and the Army of Republika Srpska hadn't been established at the time I was down there, so I'm in no position to say yes or no. If I could answer the question, I would. I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can't answer this question, which was a rather complicated question. Thank you. You may now rest for 20 minutes. We shall resume this hearing in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is back in session. Before giving the floor to Mr. Marcussen for his hour and thirty minutes of cross-examination, let me remind a few things to the witness. The witness is now a witness of justice, which means that he is not to contact anyone until tomorrow. You're still under oath until tomorrow, and the Trial Chamber is asking you not to answer any questions from the press or from anyone, to make sure that we do not run into any problem. Have you understood this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am telling you that you are now a witness of justice because you took the oath, the solemn declaration, so now you are not to contact anyone until tomorrow. Do not answer people who might be calling you on the phone, do not talk to reporters, and so forth. That way, we will not run into any problems. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, both of my phones have been disconnected since yesterday, so I haven't spoken to anyone since yesterday. I'm familiar with the rules of procedure, and that's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Congratulations, well done. Mr. Marcussen, you have an hour and thirty minutes. The Registrar will be keeping time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Jovic. My name is Mathias Marcussen. I am the senior trial attorney for the Office of the Prosecutor in this case. I am presenting myself to you because we have never met; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good day to you, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I don't believe we've ever met; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No, we've never met. Perhaps, but we didn't know each other at the time. Anything is possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I guess that's true. I wanted to ask you first: I understand that you have not been communicating with anyone since yesterday. You mentioned earlier today one of your friends, Novak Savic, who tried to help you find a job. When did you last speak to him?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Before the Chamber issued an order stating that I shouldn't speak to members of the Prosecution or members of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic -- and I'm sorry if it appears to be odd. I don't know where to be looking to be looking at you, so I'm looking down at the monitor, where I see you. So it might appear weird to you, but I'm not sort of disinterested in your questions -- in your answers. Sorry if it appears that way. I would like first to ask you about a statement that you gave to the OTP in 2006, and I would like if the usher could show you 65 ter 07330. It is in the binder that should be down in your end as well. And if it may assist, it's the binder called Binder 1, the Court binder. So, again, it's 65 ter 07330. Mr. Jovic, I see that everyone's getting ready. You're getting your glasses ready, and the usher is getting ready. How's your health?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: It's quite standard. I can now walk and communicate. I have cured some problems I had with my vertebrae, and everyone else is as it was. But my therapy, the therapy I have, is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm glad for you. Mr. Jovic, are you now able to see the statement that I talked about in your own language?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we look at the first page, is that -- is your signature on the page that you're looking at, on the first page, down at the left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And do you recognise your statement? Do you remember signing this statement in October 2006?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible. 2006, I don't know what it contains. If I have a look at its contents, I'll be able to remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Okay. We will get -- we will get to this. Maybe you will be kind enough to just look at the pages and confirm for me that your signature is at the bottom of the pages. Maybe you don't need to look at every one of the pages, but just sort of flick through and confirm that it's actually your statement -- your signature.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: It is, yes. That's it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I would like to ask you some questions about some things in the statement. You have testified today about the rally in Mali Zvornik, which ended with a brawl, and how you next, the next day, signed up as a member of the SCP. Now, you signed up because Seselj -- Seselj's speeches made a big impression on you, and that was one of the reasons why you joined the parties, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I didn't listen to Seselj's speech because he was inside the hall and I was outside, so I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But you had heard -- you had heard Seselj's speeches on television, and you were familiar with what he stood for, and that was one of the most important reasons why you joined the party; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's true that I joined because of Mali Zvornik and the brawl between the Muslims and Serbs in front of the eyes of the police force, with the policemen standing there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, the Prosecutor is using inadmissible ways of going about this. The Serbian Chetnik Movement wasn't even registered then, and it was only in December 1990 that I was allowed to appear on television. So it's not up to the Prosecutor to think things up. I wasn't on television in the 1990s -- in 1990.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, these are things the accused can raise in his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So, Mr. Jovic, are you saying that you -- what I said is not true; you did not know of Seselj's programme and had heard about his -- what he had been saying about the situation in Croatia, and that was one of the most important -- or that was the most important reason why you should join the SCP?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I said, and I'm going to repeat it again -- and don't upset me, because my blood pressure is going to soar. I joined the Serbian Chetnik Movement in 1990 because of the brawl in Mali Zvornik that broke out. So don't keep asking me the same leading questions and put words into my mouth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm asking you because if you look at paragraph 29 of the statement you have in front of you, I believe that what I've just said to you is actually coming from there. It's not something I'm making up. It's in your statement.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: You're asking me the same thing five times over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Only two, I think.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: All right, but I heard something along those lines earlier. I'll just take a moment to read it, and then I'll be able to answer. What is there bad about that? Seselj spoke up against Slobodan Milosevic. Is that a problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I have not said anything about anything being bad. I just asked you a question about why you joined the SCP, and I put to you that you did that -- one of the reasons you did that was that you had seen Seselj, you knew what he stood for, and therefore you joined the party. You disagreed with that, but do I understand now that you do agree that that was one of the important reasons why you joined?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, please believe me when I say that I wasn't a member of the Serbian Radical Party. But when all this is over, I'm going to ask to be admitted in writing. I'm going to make a written request to join.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, stay calm, and please answer the questions put to you by the Prosecution. You are a Chamber witness, and therefore Mr. Marcussen is allowed -- is entitled to put questions to you in such a way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I fully support what my fellow Judge has said. So far, up until now, this hearing ran very smoothly. You answered all questions put to you by the Judges. The Prosecutor is now doing his job. He's putting questions to you. We could have put the same questions. So please stay cool. Listen carefully to the question put to you by Mr. Marcussen and then answer just quietly and carefully. Mr. Marcussen, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, we'll move on to something else. I think you've been quite helpful on this already. Mr. Jovic, when you went back to the SCP headquarters in Belgrade for the second time before you went to Tenja, Seselj was present, and he was giving orders to Rankic, to Petkovic, and Stefanovic, and other members of the SCP staff, and he was supervising their work; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand those last two words. Could you repeat the last two words? "Supervised their work," is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That's correct. He gave ordered to them and supervised their work?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course. He was the party president, so that's quite normal if you're president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, indeed, your impression was he was in absolute control over the SCP headquarters in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did gain that impression then, but later on I saw that one party had its executive board and that they had all the institutions that are necessary to a party, because nobody can make decisions on his own about anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Right. And Seselj was addressed as "vojvoda" when you were there at that time?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Why not? Seselj was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in America, he was given the "vojvoda" baton as a mark of honour and respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So what I've just put to you comes from paragraph 27 of the statement you have in front of you, and so I believe that's actually correct, what's in the statement there. Now, in August 1991, you went to Tenja, and nobody told you how civilians were to be treated during the operations that you were to engage in; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And your impression was that -- or, actually, you, meaning, in plural, the volunteers that went, you knew that the purpose was to chase the Croatian civilians out of the village of Tenja; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I said, in answer to the first question, that you were not right, Mr. Prosecutor. You don't seem to have heard me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So I lift this from -- I put my question based on paragraph 32 of your statement that you have in front of you. So what you're telling is incorrect, what's in your statement there? Your Honours, it seems that the transmission has been disconnected, so I guess we need to have, maybe, a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marcussen, we're trying to bring the connection back up. Let's wait for the connection to be back, to be up again. Mr. Seselj, time is of the essence. I believe you had some administrative matters that you wanted to discuss. Maybe we could take advantage of this opportunity to do this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you seem to have got the connection back. Yes, I did say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Too late, the witness is back on the screen, so let's continue with the witness. Mr. Seselj, what do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have several administrative matters to raise, Mr. President, so perhaps I could raise some of them now. However, the connection seems to be established again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the line has failed again. So please go on with the administrative matters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would leave the most important matters for tomorrow. But just not to waste time, I'll raise some things now. Yesterday, I received -- well, I'll do my best, and I guarantee that I'll succeed not to say anything that shouldn't be uttered in open session, although it's not a confidential document, but to avoid us going into private session. I received an urgent request from the Prosecutor, dated the 22nd of June. It was handed over to me yesterday. I think that the request is quite nonsensical, and I think that you can see that by the title, by looking at the title. And within the space of a fortnight, I will respond in writing to that request. Next, the Prosecutor tabled a request, dated the 19th of May, which I was served on the 14th of June, saying that selected Mladic documents should be added to the court files, and I received information from the Prosecutor today that the material is available, as they say, EDB, the system for electronic data serving, and that I'll be able to find that in a scanned version of Mladic's diaries. Now, I can't seem to find that there, so we'll have to wait for the transcripts of those note-books to be completed. And the Prosecutor says that that is an ongoing process. When they'll be completed, we don't know. But I'd just like to inform you that this EDB system for electronic transmission of documents means nothing to me. I don't know what it is. Next, on the 15th of June, I received a request from the Prosecution for them to reserve the right to respond to exhibits presented to the Trial Chamber after the 1st of June, 2010. And this is the Prosecution case, so why does he want to respond to documents presented after the 1st of June? Then, once again, I have several requests from the Prosecution. I think that we have stated our positions on some of them, but I have two here, one sent on the 22nd of June, and we have not stated our position on that, the request from the Prosecution for the admittance of exhibits linked to the previous witness statements. Now, all these exhibits is something that the Prosecutor was duty-bound to present in court and then to tender them into evidence, and not to do it this way subsequently, post festum. It's a document dated the 1st of June, 2010. I was given it on the 22nd of June, and it comprises a large number of documents. Furthermore -- well, now I come to something which would take up more time, so I'm going to leave that for tomorrow, if that's all right with you, because -- well, there's another document that I was given. It's a confidential one, and so I'm going to take great care not to say anything that I shouldn't. A witness testified here in court under protective measures. And after a certain amount of time, an incident took place in a cafe, there was a brawl, in which a close relative of his took part. The local police -- it's not the Serb police that carried an on-site investigation. Anyway, they interviewed all those present, and all the citizens present were neutral, objective observers, did not mention that a close relative of the person involved in the brawl was a close relative of the protected witness. They're just describing the brawl, and it was the brother of the protected witness and the former husband -- the ex-husband of the sister were engaged in this brawl. And after this incident broke out, the police, made up of Muslims and Croats, collected statements. Those present had no idea that this person testified in my trial, and it was only relatives who made statements and said that the brawl broke out because of his testifying in this courtroom. Now, you supplied me with all the documents. I have reviewed them, and I am astounded that something like that is possible at all. So that means that anybody in future closely related or distance relatives, if they enter into any conflict or brawl, whether they're right or wrong, everything will be linked to their possible testimony at this trial, whereas the Muslim and Croat who sent you these statements, they claim that this has -- that this is connected to the secret testimony during this trial. I think, Your Honours, that you have read through the material, you know all about this incident, and that there's no need for me to go into the details of what is contained in those documents. And after you studied them, you handed the documents to me so that I could become acquainted with the contents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We took due note of what you said. Yesterday, we issued four decisions. They were filed, but I believe that you did not get them yet because they have to be translated. I hope that you will soon have them. The witness is still not on the screen, so we do have a problem. Mr. Seselj, I'll take advantage of this opportunity to think about the future. You know that this is our last witness. After this, we will enter into a new phase, Rule 98 bis phase. But as you mentioned earlier, there's still some pending motions, notably those dealing with the Mladic diaries, and I'm sure that in some time the Prosecution will tell us exactly what its position is, and the Chamber will rule on it. All this will take time. So after scrutinising the schedule as it is, I don't think that we can start the Rule 98 bis hearing before September, before early September. Furthermore, the Rule in Article 65 ter of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, it says, and I will read it slowly, but I'm sure you know it as well as the Judges do, this is a public hearing, so we might as well inform the public at large, Article 65 ter (G) of the Regulation says the following: "After the presentation of the Prosecution case and before the presentation of the Defence case, the Pre-Trial Judge," and for those who might have forgotten, let me remind you that it was myself, and as Presiding Judge, I can appoint the Pre-Trial Judge or appoint myself, "orders the Defence to disclose a list of witnesses that the Defence wishes to call, stating: the name or pseudonym of each of these witnesses; a summary of the facts that each witness will testify on; the items in the indictment on which each witness will be heard; the number of witnesses; and the number of witnesses who will testify on each count; whether the witness will testify viva voce or according to Rule 92 bis or 92 quater. There might be a need for a written statement or a transcript of previous testimony." And then: "F. The estimated time for each testimony." And then: "2. A list of all exhibits that the Defence wishes to present to support its case." So as you see, you are legally bound to prepare all this and to tell us your witness list, with the name of each witness, the time you request for each witness, and so forth and so on. I would like to know whether you've already started working on this and whether today you can shed some light on what you're about to do.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, why would I work at that now? According to 98 bis, you make the judgement. And on the basis of that judgement, you size up the results of the Prosecution case. There is the theoretical possibility that that be completely an exculpatory judgement, a judgement before acquittal. Why should I put the cart before the horse and engage all my scant resources, because the people who help me out are not paid, so why should I resort to that now? Now, judging by the success scored by the Prosecution thus far, you can bring in a complete judgement of acquittal. Now, I'm not a naive man, myself. I know that not everything depends on your will, because even if there is an intimation of the possibility where I might find myself at liberty, there's general panic in Belgrade. Many people panic; the regime, the opposition, those play-acting at being the opposition. But that's another matter. Now, under Rule 98 bis, you first of all listened to the individual parties. We discussed this issue last time, and I said that I need about four hours, which is as much as Mr. Marcussen asked for, but we didn't actually consult the Rule. Now, since you are listening to the two parties, Mr. Marcussen will state his views first and then I go second, because the Prosecutor goes first and the accused goes second, and then it's up to you to make your judgement. And once you have judged, you can either confirm that the Prosecutor was successful, judging by mostly your opinions, or you can judge that he was not successful and make a judgement of acquittal. But judging by this 92 bis, you first of all -- we now seem to have a musical accompaniment. I don't really like this music. Can you hear the music or have I gone mad? But there is certainly some music that we can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, there is music in the background. So before continuing --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't like this sort of music accompaniment. I like Serb folk music, so if they play that to me, I can sing a song. I can sing you some Chetnik songs, too, but I just don't like this music. It doesn't suit me. But I want to act properly towards you, and for me to do that, I cannot present my Defence case until you resolve the matter of finance. If I'm not paid, in conformity with case law so far and the practice at this Tribunal, in the pre-trial phase and in the trial phase, if I'm not able to pay my associates, they won't want to work for me anymore, and that will bring the trial to an end straight away. Now, you informed me that the Registrar has received eight documents regarding my material -- my financial status. I haven't seen those documents yet, but I assume that the Registrar has a complete picture of my finances. However, the Registrar is trying to trick me all the time, bringing in new rules, as if I'm interested in these new rules, the new rules enacted by the Registrar. I adhere to the Statute and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, and, in my view, it's only the Trial Chamber that can make decisions of that kind and not the Registrar. The Registrar takes it into his head to bring in new provisions and rules and I should adapt. I'm not going to adapt. I provided all the data about my property in 2003, and as far as I'm concerned, that closes the issue. You know how much the Defence before this Tribunal costs, on the basis of what it cost at other trials. I am the third-most serious category. You know how much the pre-trial phase costs and how much the trial phase costs. And as I'm my own lawyer, you can deduct half of that, because I'm not going to ask the Tribunal to pay me for my services for defending myself. And it's about half what other lawyers receive in other trials, but the other half has to be paid out to my associates on the basis of what they've done, and the work they've done can be proved on the basis of their written submissions. They did much more than any other lawyer in the pre-trial phase, and they've supplied me very successfully with material in this stage of the Tribunal. So I was far more successful than the Prosecutor. And so many Prosecutors have changed places here, 10 of them, but I've dealt with all of them and brought them down to their knees, as the Serbs like to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, the witness is back on the screen. It seems that the connection is up again. We'll continue with this tomorrow. I'm sure we'll have some time to discuss pending items, but we can continue. Mr. Marcussen, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you -- when you were in Tenja, you were with a unit from the SCP; right? Mr. Jovic, could you hear my question or do we have another technical problem?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but -- I heard you, but I thought you were going to ask me something after that. Yes, I was in the Movement of the Serbian -- I was in the Serbian Chetnik Movement in Tenja.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But you left that unit because you didn't like the people, because there were some thefts in the unit and people drank a lot; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not true, that's not true. I have already repeated why I left. You have to put your questions, so I respect that, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And eventually the unit was sent away from Tenja because the TO commander could not control them anymore; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. They were transferred for strategic needs. They were transferred to another location that I'm not aware of, because I wasn't part of the command staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So you're saying that -- maybe we don't need to go to it, but I'm putting my questions because this is the contents of paragraphs 39 and 41 of your statement. Now, let me put to you another question from your statement. You had joined the SCP, but you realised that, actually, Seselj and Milosevic were working together; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: It's not true. Who said that, who inserted that? Where does that -- where can that be found?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It can be found in paragraph 52 of your statement, and also in paragraph 13.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I'll find it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I take your question [sic]. You're saying this is -- this is not correct. I take your answer, that it's not correct. I think the Trial Chamber has heard that answer.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: It's certainly not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, from December to March 19 -- from December 1991 to March 1992, you participated in three transports of weapons from Darda to the Zvornik area; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Sorry, could you repeat that? That didn't come through, what you said. Sorry, we couldn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I said that that is correct. I don't know the dates, however, because I didn't participate in them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I think there's a confusion. You participated in three weapons transports; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I said correct.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said, "I participated in that, I said correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you went to Darda, the chief of police from Zvornik and you met with Radoslav Kostic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the police commander, not the chief. The chief of police was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. And Kostic was a member of the Serbian State Security Service; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No. Kostic was Martic's deputy. He was the deputy minister for Slavonia and Baranja and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And during one of these -- one of the occasion you were up to fetch weapons, you heard a conversation between the police -- I apologise -- the police commander from Zvornik and Kostic, where the police commander said that Radmilo Bogdanovic had promised more weapons; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: One could say so, and for weapons that were better, of better quality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And so in the weapons transports where you participated, four or five truckloads of weapons were brought back to the Zvornik area; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No, not that many. I can't remember how many exactly. A lot of time has passed since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you saw Radoslav Kostic drive a red BMW with police state security license plates; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: An SDB vehicle? I'm not familiar with any such vehicle. What does it say on the registration plates? Could someone tell me? It says "State Security?" Does it say "State Security"? You'd have people shooting on it. There was a civilian Golf with a registration number for Bijeli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm referring to paragraph 66 of your statement, where it says: "I assumed that Kostic held a high position because he drove a State Security car, a dark red BMW with Police State Security plates."

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: 66, is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: He was superior to someone else because he had a better car, he drove a better car. Radoslav Kostic drove a Golf car with registration plates for Beli Manastir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So the statement here is not true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Certain things have been inserted. It's partially true I recognise, or I admit that certain things were true. I did say that I escorted these weapons. That's true and that's what I said, but I won't lie here. I'm not going to concern things that are not true before the Tribunal and the Chamber. Rita should justify this, explain this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You also met a person called Marko Pavlovic when you were in Darda for the weapons transports; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I met someone -- not him, but quite a few people, and he was among those whom I met.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And Marko Pavlovic was a subordinate of Kostic; right?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they were friends. I don't know. You couldn't say that he stood in front of him peacefully. They were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In paragraph 66 of your statement, you say: "My assumption is that Marko Pavlovic and Dragan Spasojevic were on the same level, and that Kostic was superior to both."

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Kostic was in his territory in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. He was the deputy minister. Of course, he was superior to everyone in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. I wouldn't be in such a position. Don't hold it against me if I put it this way. And I apologise for what I said a little earlier on. I have high blood pressure, so it's sometimes difficult for me to control myself. But we can continue discussing matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Not to worry. The weapons that you brought back from Darda were stored in the Zvornik area, and then in March and April they were distributed by the SDS Party to local Serbs from various villages in and around Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Naturally, but I have to add that these weapons were old weapons from the Territorial Defence, weapons that had been written off. There were old rifles and so on and so forth. There was nothing new, nothing very lethal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when those --

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Why this person complained and said, Why isn't there anything new, since the person -- or, rather, the man said that there were such weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And the weapons that were brought in were brought in because preparations were ongoing for war; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, because the Patriotic League had already been established. The Muslims were armed to the teeth at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in April 1992, war did, indeed, break out. And as you have explained earlier, you participated in the -- on the Serbian side during the attack on Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Before the actual attack started, you went to Hotel Jezero in Mali Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't receive any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You were sent to Hotel Jezero in Mali Zvornik by the commander of the police, for whom you were the bodyguard, is that correct, right before the attack?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it's about. Ask me quite freely. I'll tell you, because the Jezero Hotel, I spent time there all the time; now, too. So are you referring to negotiations with the Serbs? If that is what you have in mind, please tell me, and I will tell you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That is what I have in mind. You were sent there to arrest the delegates, a number of the delegates, in those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, to take them from the hall to a flat on a floor. The commander issued this order to me, Spasojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you were told to take the members of the delegation to Room 101; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it was 101. I've forgotten. It was a long time ago. That's possible, but I did take them to the flat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, actually, that room, or that flat, as you call it, had been reserved for Marko Pavlovic and Kostic; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Anything is possible, but I have no information about that. Perhaps -- perhaps that's why they sent them there, but I have no information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that the room had been reserved for those two men, and that the manager of the hotel was shocked that you knew because it was supposed to be secret. And that's in paragraph 86 of your statement. But let's move on. At one point --

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it's possible. Let's say that that's how it was, because -- well, what are you asking me now? Can I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's possible that the statement is correct? Actually, you don't think it's incorrect?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not saying that it's incorrect. I'm not sure. A lot of time has passed since then, and many things have been forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you were guarding the delegation, and then at one point Arkan came into the room?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And later on, you overheard -- you overheard Arkan give the Muslim participants in the delegation an ultimatum, that they should evacuate Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And later on --

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: It was his position at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So Arkan issued an ultimatum. Now, Arkan had come to -- had come to the Zvornik area sometime before at the request of the commander of the police; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know with whom he was reaching an agreement. I really don't know. But it is a fact that he appeared there, but from Zvornik, in Bosnia, not from Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Right. He was on the Serbian side of the Drina River, and there he set up a base before the attack; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: No one could prevent him from doing this, forbid him. He would go where he wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you were familiar with this, and you knew that he was there because he was planning the attack on Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't know that an attack on Zvornik was being planned. When the barricades went up in Zvornik, then one saw what was going to happen. But I was there when the delegation was present in the hotel. There were Serbian negotiators and there were Muslim negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And following the ultimatum by Arkan, he, that is, Arkan, also commanded the operation that was carried out by the Serb forces to take over Zvornik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: That's not correct. Arkan commanded his unit. The other Serbian forces were part of the Crisis Staff of the Serbs who lived in Bosnia at the time. Now, it is Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You say in your statement that: "During the attack, you all came under Arkan's command. He led the operation, although the decision must have been reached at the headquarters when the commanders, including Arkan, met." So -- and that is in paragraph 93 of your statement. So there you say that Arkan was in the overall operational command of the operation; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, you said something which I think the interpreters were not able to catch, so maybe you can repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: To see about that, I have to read that. I have to read it and see what it says exactly. Is this in English? You said paragraph 23; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: 93. It's partially correct. It's not correct to say that he was in command of the entire operation for the liberation of Zvornik, but it's true that he was in command of a group that was with him at the barricades on the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So he was in command of you?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was my commander. I was a member of the MUP, but the MUP in Bosnia and Herzegovina. I was a mobilised policeman, and that's it. So he didn't have command over that unit. He was quite simply there when we set off. He returned. He didn't advance with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 92 of your statement that: "The group that were involved in the attack included 50 of Seselj's Chetniks." I think you've said something different today, but isn't it true that there were 50 of Seselj's Chetniks or members of the SDS SIS involved in the attack?

utterances.speaker: NENAD JOVIC
utterances.text: That's note true. I can claim with full responsibility that these were members of Zvornik, Karakaj, and other surrounding villages. I know those people. I live a kilometre from where they live, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Mr. Jovic, I have to tell you that I have the distinction impression that your statement is correct except when there is any mention of Seselj in the statement. Can you help me understand that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need to put a question to the witness. You say that these were locals, but were they nonetheless connected in some way to the Serbian Radical Party, because they might have been members of the Serbian Radical Party or recruited by the Serbian Radical Party, sympathisers of the Serbian Radical Party, perhaps, even if they did not come from Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They didn't have their own commander. They weren't organised. They followed Arkan because they saw that there was someone in command there. So they went there of their own free will. But when the Prosecution says that I'm lying whenever -- please listen to me. Let me say this. If you say that I'm lying, well, I'll lie, but you have to say this in public. I'm telling you the truth, though, and I've taken a solemn declaration, I'm under oath. No one is going to humiliate me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, perhaps we have not understood each other well. I'm not saying that you are lying. This is not what is in issue. We addressed -- or the Prosecutor put questions to you about a different group. This was not Arkan's group. This was another group, a group which is mentioned in the statement you gave the OTP, which you characterised as being members of the Serbian Radical Party, Seseljevci, Seselj's men. So my question relates to this group. This is why I wanted to ask you this. You said that they came from the neighbouring villages when the attack on Zvornik took place, so you wanted to say that they did not come from Serbia. I understood this. This is what I understood you to say, that these people did not come from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, please explain to me, what does the scum group mean, Seselj's scum group? Do you know what "scum" "means? Do you know what the word "schlum" [phoen] means in Serbian, "scum"? The interpretation I received was "the scum group."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what that is. I said "Seseljevci, Seselj's men."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard "the schlamovi [phoen] group." In English, "the scum group, Seselj's group, Seselj's men. "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to say something about the interpreters. You must be extremely careful when you interpret. My colleague never discussed scum. Why is it that in B/C/S, this is translated as "scum"? Judge Lattanzi talked about Seselj's men. I would like to caution the interpreters when they are working. Thank you. The witness has just said, himself, that he heard the word "scum" in his own language. This has never been said either by Mr. Marcussen or Judge Lattanzi. Witness, are you quite sure that you heard this in your language, the word "scum"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm certain I heard the word "schlum" or "scum," "Seselj's men, scum." I'm certain about that. I have the impression that someone wants to irritate me because they can see that I'm ill, that I am a little bit on edge, so please protect me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I am protecting you. If I step in, it is because I have discovered a problem. It will be a very serious matter to translate "scum" when no one has ever mentioned the word. I would like the person in charge of the interpretation services at the Tribunal to check this out and check the soundtrack. This is a digression. It is now 7.00 p.m. We need to stop. Witness, you can stop. This is tiring to answer questions, as you can see. Have a good rest. We shall meet again tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 p.m. Mr. Marcussen will finish his cross-examination, and after that Mr. Seselj will have an hour and a half to put questions to you. So these are my instructions. Have a good rest, and be fit and well for tomorrow. I hope you have understood me well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you all the best as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wish you, as well as everyone in the courtroom, a pleasant evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 7th day of July, 2010, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.01 p.m.,
